🔮 Small-Caps (Russell 2000) — Front-Running Eventual Rate Relief
 What the market is pricing in: Russell 2000 at 3,011 is outperforming Nasdaq 100 (Russell/Nasdaq ratio ↑1.6% vs 4W) despite yields surging.
This is unusual — small-caps are rate-sensitive and should underperform in a rising-yield environment.

Retail investors are telling themselves a simple, emotionally irresistible story: yields are surging (10Y at 4.67%, climbing), the dollar's trajectory is uncertain, geopolitical risk is front-page (Iran deal negotiations dominating headlines), mortgage rates just hit their highest levels in over a year, and professional commentators are warning that "one of the longest winning streaks in stock market history is coming to an end." The Gold/Copper ratio at 641 — flagged as FEAR-elevated — validates the gut feeling: this isn't a commodity boom, this is a fear bid.
The move is occurring even as Treasury yields surge (10Y up 3.0% over four weeks to 4.67%), which historically would be a headwind for non-yielding gold.

The fact that gold is climbing despite rising yields signals something structural: the traditional inverse correlation has broken, and retail reads this as confirmation that the old playbook is dead and gold is re-pricing for a new monetary regime.

Many macro funds are long gold as a structural allocation — the central-bank-buying and de-dollarization theses have fundamental support, and the breaking of the gold-yield inverse correlation suggests a regime change that institutions acknowledge.

A sharp reversal in Treasury yields (currently surging) driven by stronger-than-expected jobs data from the July report — which the market was eyeing this week — could also crack the thesis by reasserting the traditional "rising real yields = gold down" relationship.
